Pleasure... man, I... I'm not really sure how to answer that. I honestly don't know. I guess I just haven't noticed one way or the other, mostly because... well, I don't really do any of the stuff I used to do anyway. 

Like, before that contract changed and my hours got all crazy, I used to spend a lot of time out in my garage. I have this old wooden workbench my father-in-law helped me build when we first bought the house, and I’d be out there fixing up small engines, you know, old push mowers or chainsaws that people were throwing out. It was peaceful. I'd put on the classic rock station, grab a cold beer from the mini-fridge, and just tinker for hours on a Saturday. But now? I couldn't tell you if I'd still enjoy it because I haven't even stepped foot in that part of the garage in I don't know how long. The tools are probably sitting there gathering an inch of dust by now. 

Same with fishing. I used to love taking my boys out to the reservoir on Sunday mornings. We’d pack a cooler, get some nightcrawlers, and get out there early before the sun got too hot... but I haven't taken them in so long. My wife, she asks me sometimes, "Hey, why don't you go work on that carburetor?" or "Why don't you take the kids down to the lake today?" and I just... I don't know. I just tell her I'm good, and I sit in my recliner. 

So if you're asking if those things still bring me pleasure, I honestly couldn't give you a straight yes or no. I just haven't tried them to find out. I come home, I drop my muddy boots by the door, and I just stare at the TV without really watching whatever is on. So I really don't know if the enjoyment is actually gone, or if I'm just... not doing them to begin with. It's just a big blank to me now.

I mean... interest? That's... it's kind of like what I was just saying about the pleasure part, doc. I don't even really know how to separate the two, or if I even have an answer for you. 

If you asked my wife, she'd probably say yes, absolutely, he doesn't care about a single thing anymore. But from inside my own head? I just don't know. I used to be the guy who had the sharpest edges along the driveway, the thickest, greenest grass. I’d be out there on a Sunday evening, off the clock, just making sure every single blade was perfect. I'd be checking the sprinkler heads, adjusting the timers, making sure the fertilizer was laid down just right for the season. I cared a lot. I really, really did. It was a huge point of pride for me, having the other guys on the block ask me what my secret was. 

But now... I drive up to the house after a 12-hour shift, and I can see the dandelions creeping up around the mailbox. I can see the edges along the sidewalk getting shaggy and overgrown, and I just look at it and feel... nothing. I don't feel that old urge to go grab the edger and fix it, but I also haven't consciously decided that I don't care. I just look at it, I walk past it, I go inside, wash the dirt off my hands, and sit in my chair. 

So, have I lost interest? I honestly couldn't tell you for sure. Maybe? Or maybe I'm just too completely hollowed out to muster up the energy it takes to care about anything. It's really hard to tell the difference between not having an interest and just running on completely empty, you know? It's all just this big, heavy gray fog where my drive used to be, so I really don't know what to call it.

Guilty... huh. You know, doc, that's a funny word to use right now. I mean, if you look at it from the outside, a guy like me—a husband, a father—I probably *should* feel guilty, right?

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Ending my life? No... no, doc, I can't say that I have. 

I know people probably think that when you're stuck in this... whatever this is, this big gray fog... that you must want to just pull the plug on everything. But honestly? Thinking about ending it all... that takes a kind of effort. It takes a certain kind of... I don't know, a sharp kind of pain or desperation that I just don't have in me right now. 

Like, I see guys on my crew sometimes, the younger guys, and they get all worked up over a bad breakup or a blown transmission in their truck, and they're yelling and throwing wrenches or kicking the tires... they have that fire, you know? Even if it's a negative fire, they feel something strongly enough to act out. If I was going to actually sit down and think about ending my life, I feel like I'd need some kind of fire to push me to do it. I'd need to feel so actively miserable that I'd want to escape. But like I was saying about the lawn, and the fishing, and listening to my wife making dinner... I'm just running on completely empty. 

I wake up, I put on my work boots, I go out and lay mulch or run the zero-turn mower for twelve hours in the blazing sun, and I come home and sit in that recliner. I don't want to die, but it's not like I'm exactly thrilled to be alive either, if that makes sense? It's just... existing. Like a ghost haunting my own living room. I don't have the energy to want to end it. I don't sit there planning anything or looking at the rafters in my garage thinking about how to check out early. I just sit there waiting for the clock to run out on the day so I can go to sleep, and then I get up and do it all over again the next morning. 

So no, I haven't thought about actually doing anything to myself. It's just... it would be too much work to even wrap my head around a plan like that. I'm just here. Taking up space, I guess.

Moving or speaking slower? Hmm... well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my knees pop a little louder when I get out of the truck these days, but that's just because I'm forty-eight and I've been doing hard physical labor since I was eighteen, you know? You see, out on the job site, you can't really afford to move slow. If we've got a contract to lay down three pallets of sod before a thunderstorm rolls in, I'm out there hustling just like the rest of the crew. I'm still swinging the weed whacker, still loading up the trailer, still driving the skid steer at the exact same pace I always have. It might feel like a heavier lift in my head, like I'm dragging a chain behind me mentally just to get through the afternoon, but if you were just standing on the sidewalk watching me work, I look exactly the same as I did ten years ago. I'm not moving like a turtle or anything. 

And as far as talking goes... well, I guess you can hear me right now, doc. I don't think my words are coming out any slower than they used to. Now, I might not have as much to actually *say* to folks anymore. It used to be that me and the guys would shoot the breeze all morning, talking about the football game or complaining about the price of gas, and now... I don't know, I just kind of give them their assignments. I'll say, "Hey, you grab the edger, I'll take the zero-turn," and then I just put my ear protection on and tune it all out. But the actual speed of my voice? The way the words come out of my mouth? Nah, that hasn't changed at all. 

It's really just like I was saying before about the engine. It's not that the engine runs slow once it's on. The RPMs are exactly the same. It's just that I don't want to turn the key in the ignition in the first place. But once I'm up and moving, I'm moving at a normal speed. I just stop the absolute second I don't have to be moving anymore, and I sink right back into that recliner. So, no, I haven't noticed any kind of physical slow-down in how I walk or talk. Just... a slow-down in caring about doing either of them, I guess.

Over three years of just waking up and feeling completely drained before I even lace up my work boots, and it just feels like there's no end in sight to it.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy before these feelings started?\n\nPatient: Pleasure... man, I... I'm not really sure how to answer that. I honestly don't know. I guess I just haven't noticed one way or the other, mostly because... well, I don't really do any of the stuff I used to do anyway. \n\nLike, before that contract changed and my hours got all crazy, I used to spend a lot of time out in my garage. I have this old wooden workbench my father-in-law helped me build when we first bought the house, and I’d be out there fixing up small engines, you know, old push mowers or chainsaws that people were throwing out. It was peaceful. I'd put on the classic rock station, grab a cold beer from the mini-fridge, and just tinker for hours on a Saturday. But now? I couldn't tell you if I'd still enjoy it because I haven't even stepped foot in that part of the garage in I don't know how long. The tools are probably sitting there gathering an inch of dust by now. \n\nSame with fishing. I used to love taking my boys out to the reservoir on Sunday mornings. We’d pack a cooler, get some nightcrawlers, and get out there early before the sun got too hot... but I haven't taken them in so long. My wife, she asks me sometimes, \"Hey, why don't you go work on that carburetor?\" or \"Why don't you take the kids down to the lake today?\" and I just... I don't know. I just tell her I'm good, and I sit in my recliner. \n\nSo if you're asking if those things still bring me pleasure, I honestly couldn't give you a straight yes or no. I just haven't tried them to find out. I come home, I drop my muddy boots by the door, and I just stare at the TV without really watching whatever is on. So I really don't know if the enjoyment is actually gone, or if I'm just... not doing them to begin with. It's just a big blank to me now.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to care about?\n\nPatient: I mean... interest? I'd be checking the sprinkler heads, adjusting the timers, making sure the fertilizer was laid down just right for the season. I cared a lot. I really, really did. I drive up to the house after a 12-hour shift, and I can see the dandelions creeping up around the mailbox. Or maybe I'm just too completely hollowed out to muster up the energy it takes to care about anything. It's really hard to tell the difference between not having an interest and just running on completely empty, you know? It's all just this big, heavy gray fog where my drive used to be, so I really don't know what to call it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about anything in particular?\n\nPatient: Guilty... huh. That sharp, awful feeling in your gut that tells you you're messing up. \n\nBut now? Man, I just... I don't feel that pit. I don't feel the sting of it at all. I don't know, a sharp kind of pain or desperation that I just don't have in me right now. \n\nLike, I see guys on my crew sometimes, the younger guys, and they get all worked up over a bad breakup or a blown transmission in their truck, and they're yelling and throwing wrenches or kicking the tires... they have that fire, you know? I'm just running on completely empty. \n\nI wake up, I put on my work boots, I go out and lay mulch or run the zero-turn mower for twelve hours in the blazing sun, and I come home and sit in that recliner. I don't have the energy to want to end it. I don't sit there planning anything or looking at the rafters in my garage thinking about how to check out early. I just sit there waiting for the clock to run out on the day so I can go to sleep, and then I get up and do it all over again the next morning. \n\nSo no, I haven't thought about actually doing anything to myself. It's just... it would be too much work to even wrap my head around a plan like that. I'm just here. Sleep? No, I... I can't say I've noticed anything different there. My sleep is pretty much exactly what it’s always been. 

I mean, you gotta figure, with the kind of work I do, sleep isn't really something I have to think about or try to do. It just happens to me. I don't toss and turn, doc. I don't lay there with my mind racing or worrying about things, because like I said, I just don't have the energy to care enough to worry. My head hits the pillow and it's just... black. Just a heavy, blank kind of sleep. I don't even dream, or if I do, I sure don't remember them. I sleep straight through the night, every single night. 

And then the alarm goes off at 4:45 AM. It buzzes, I reach over and hit the button, and I sit up. I don't hit snooze, I don't lay there wishing for five more minutes, I just put my feet on the floor, put my work boots on, and start the whole gray day all over again. So, no, the pattern hasn't changed at all in three years, or even ten years. It's the exact same hours, the exact same heavy sleep. It's just a pause button, really. Just shutting the machine down for a few hours before I have to turn the key again. But the actual sleep itself? No changes at all.

I'm a landscaper, right? So for years, my own yard had to be the absolute showcase of the neighborhood. I used to be the guy who had the sharpest edges along the driveway, the thickest, greenest grass. I’d be out there on a Sunday evening, off the clock, just making sure every single blade was perfect. I'd be checking the sprinkler heads, adjusting the timers, making sure the fertilizer was laid down just right for the season. I cared a lot. I really, really did. It was a huge point of pride for me, having the other guys on the block ask me what my secret was. \n\nBut now... I drive up to the house after a 12-hour shift, and I can see the dandelions creeping up around the mailbox. I can see the edges along the sidewalk getting shaggy and overgrown, and I just look at it and feel... nothing. I don't feel that old urge to go grab the edger and fix it, but I also haven't consciously decided that I don't care. I just look at it, I walk past it, I go inside, wash the dirt off my hands, and sit in my chair. \n\nSo, have I lost interest? I honestly couldn't tell you for sure. Maybe? Or maybe I'm just too completely hollowed out to muster up the energy it takes to care about anything. It's really hard to tell the difference between not having an interest and just running on completely empty, you know? It's all just this big, heavy gray fog where my drive used to be, so I really don't know what to call it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about anything in particular?\n\nPatient: Guilty... huh. You know, doc, that's a funny word to use right now. I'll be sitting there after work, and I can hear my wife in the kitchen. She's clanking the pots and pans around, trying to get dinner together after she's already been going hard all day herself, and the boys are in the living room asking her for help with their homework or arguing over something, and I'm just... sitting there. Staring at the wall or the TV. There are gutters that need cleaning out, the truck probably needs an oil change, the whole nine yards. \n\nNow, you go back, say, four or five years ago, before all this started? If I had just sat on my behind while my wife did everything, I would have felt like the absolute worst piece of garbage on the planet. I would have had this massive pit in my stomach, just eating away at me, telling me, \"Get up, be a man, help your family out.\" That's what guilt is, right? That sharp, awful feeling in your gut that tells you you're messing up. \n\nBut now? Man, I just... I don't feel that pit. I don't feel the sting of it at all. I can sit there and listen to her doing everything, and I know in my head—logically, you know?—that I should be helping, that I should feel bad for leaving it all on her shoulders. But the actual feeling of guilt just doesn't show up. It's like the part of me that's supposed to feel bad about letting people down is just as broken and numb as the part that used to care about my front lawn. It's just flat. I don't feel bad, I don't feel good, I just feel too completely drained to have any sort of emotion about it one way or the other. So no, I wouldn't say I feel guilty about anything. I just don't have the energy to even feel bad anymore. It's just more of that same empty fog.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about ending your life?\n\nPatient: Ending my life? I don't know, a sharp kind of pain or desperation that I just don't have in me right now. \n\nLike, I see guys on my crew sometimes, the younger guys, and they get all worked up over a bad breakup or a blown transmission in their truck, and they're yelling and throwing wrenches or kicking the tires... they have that fire, you know? Even if it's a negative fire, they feel something strongly enough to act out. If I was going to actually sit down and think about ending my life, I feel like I'd need some kind of fire to push me to do it. I'd need to feel so actively miserable that I'd want to escape. But like I was saying about the lawn, and the fishing, and listening to my wife making dinner... I'm just running on completely empty. \n\nI wake up, I put on my work boots, I go out and lay mulch or run the zero-turn mower for twelve hours in the blazing sun, and I come home and sit in that recliner. I don't want to die, but it's not like I'm exactly thrilled to be alive either, if that makes sense? It's just... existing. Like a ghost haunting my own living room. I don't have the energy to want to end it. I don't sit there planning anything or looking at the rafters in my garage thinking about how to check out early. I just sit there waiting for the clock to run out on the day so I can go to sleep, and then I get up and do it all over again the next morning. \n\nSo no, I haven't thought about actually doing anything to myself. It's just... it would be too much work to even wrap my head around a plan like that. I'm just here. Taking up space, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your weight over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Weight? No, I... I don't think so. But as far as I can tell, I’m sitting at about the exact same weight I’ve always been. \n\nYou gotta understand, doc, with the line of work I'm in, it's pretty physical. They get holes in the knees from the dirt and the gravel, and I just go down to the tractor supply store and buy the exact same pair, same size, and they always button up just fine. So my waistline hasn't really moved an inch either way. \n\nAnd it's not like my eating habits have really shifted, either. Like I was saying before, I come home, wash the dirt off, sit in that recliner, and whatever my wife puts on a plate in front of me, I just eat it. I don't even really taste it half the time anymore. It's just fuel, you know? Just putting gas in the tank so the engine turns over the next morning. She could put a nice steak down, or she could put down a bowl of plain white rice, and I'd eat it exactly the same way, at the exact same speed. I don't go back for seconds because I don't care enough to get up and walk back into the kitchen, and I don't skip meals because she'd get on my case about it and ask me if I was feeling sick, and I just don't have the energy to have that conversation. I just eat what's there. \n\nEven at work, sometimes the guys on the crew will stop at a gas station between jobs and grab those roller hot dogs or a bag of chips, and I'll grab something too, just because it's what we do at 11 AM on a Tuesday. It's all just routine. You just go through the motions of eating because that's what people do when the clock hits a certain hour. So, no, I haven't noticed any weight changes. I haven't gained a gut, haven't shrunk down to skin and bones. I'm just exactly the same as I was three years ago. Just... stuck right in the exact same spot, wearing the exact same pants, eating the exact same amount of food without even really thinking about it.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Moving or speaking slower? Hmm... well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my knees pop a little louder when I get out of the truck these days, but that's just because I'm forty-eight and I've been doing hard physical labor since I was eighteen, you know? But actual slow motion? No, I don't think so. \n\nYou see, out on the job site, you can't really afford to move slow. If we've got a contract to lay down three pallets of sod before a thunderstorm rolls in, I'm out there hustling just like the rest of the crew. I'm still swinging the weed whacker, still loading up the trailer, still driving the skid steer at the exact same pace I always have. It might feel like a heavier lift in my head, like I'm dragging a chain behind me mentally just to get through the afternoon, but if you were just standing on the sidewalk watching me work, I look exactly the same as I did ten years ago. I'm not moving like a turtle or anything. \n\nAnd as far as talking goes... well, I guess you can hear me right now, doc. I don't think my words are coming out any slower than they used to. Now, I might not have as much to actually *say* to folks anymore. I don't know, I just kind of give them their assignments. I'll say, \"Hey, you grab the edger, I'll take the zero-turn,\" and then I just put my ear protection on and tune it all out. It's not that the engine runs slow once it's on. The RPMs are exactly the same. It's just that I don't want to turn the key in the ignition in the first place. But once I'm up and moving, I'm moving at a normal speed. I just stop the absolute second I don't have to be moving anymore, and I sink right back into that recliner. So, no, I haven't noticed any kind of physical slow-down in how I walk or talk. Just... a slow-down in caring about doing either of them, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns over the past three years?\n\nPatient: Sleep? No, I... I can't say I've noticed anything different there. My sleep is pretty much exactly what it’s always been. \n\nI mean, you gotta figure, with the kind of work I do, sleep isn't really something I have to think about or try to do. When you've been on your feet for ten, twelve hours, wrestling with a commercial mower or hauling yard waste into the back of a dump trailer, your body doesn't really give you a choice by the time evening rolls around. So my pattern is just... well, it's set in stone. Has been for years. \n\nLike I was telling you before about my evening routine... I get home, I eat whatever my wife puts in front of me, and I sit in that recliner. By about 9:00, 9:15, I can feel the physical exhaustion just sort of pulling me down into the cushions. We usually have the TV on, maybe some local news or one of those home improvement shows my wife likes, but I'm not really watching it. I'm just staring at the colors moving on the screen. And then at 9:30, on the dot, I push myself up out of the chair, walk down the hall, brush my teeth, and get into bed. \n\nI don't toss and turn, doc. It buzzes, I reach over and hit the button, and I sit up. Focusing? No, I don't think so. I mean, my mind doesn't wander off or anything like that. If I'm doing a job, I'm locked in on the job. 

Like, just to give you an idea... if we're putting in a new paver patio, right? You can't just lose focus on a job like that. It's precision work. You have to excavate down at least seven or eight inches, lay down the compacted gravel base, and then you have to screed the sand. And when you're screeding that sand, you have to maintain a very specific slope away from the house—usually about a quarter inch of drop for every foot of run—otherwise, the first heavy rain we get, all that water is just going to pool right up against the client's foundation and flood their basement. If I couldn't pay attention, I'd be messing up that grade all the time. But I don't. I run the string line, I check the bubble on my level every couple of feet, I do the math in my head to make sure the pitch is exactly right. I can stand there and calculate exactly how many square feet we've got, how many pallets of stone we need to pull from the supplier, how many bags of polymeric sand it's going to take to lock the joints... all of that. My brain works fine for all the details. 

And it's the same with driving. I drive an F-250 pulling a sixteen-foot double-axle trailer loaded down with zero-turn mowers and aerators all day. You try backing one of those rigs into a narrow, curved driveway in a high-end subdivision with cars parked on both sides of the street. If you lose your focus for even two seconds doing that, you're taking out a brick mailbox or side-swiping somebody's Mercedes. But my driving record is completely clean. Haven't had a single ding in, gosh, probably over a decade. 

So, no, the attention is there. I know exactly what I'm doing, and I don't lose track of my thoughts or forget what I'm working on. It's just... like I was saying before, it's the weight of it. I can stare at that string line and know exactly how to lay the next row of pavers, my mind is completely clear on the task, but getting my body to actually bend down, pick up the eight-pound block, and set it in the sand... it just feels like this monumental, draining effort. The focus isn't the problem at all, doc. It's just having the energy to actually act on what I'm focusing on.

Before the contract change? No, doc, not at all. I mean, sure, in this line of work you always have days where your back aches or you just want to sleep through Sunday, but this... this heavy, empty feeling? No. That's entirely tied to when everything shifted with the business. 

If I look back, I can pinpoint it pretty much exactly. It’s been going on for about three years and three months now. That was right around the time the big commercial groundskeeping contract we had came up for renewal, and the property management company decided they wanted to completely change our schedule. They had all these new stipulations, right? They decided they didn't want our mowers running while their office staff were doing meetings or having phone calls, so suddenly we couldn't run the heavy machinery during normal business hours. We either had to be there at the absolute crack of dawn, like 4:30 in the morning, working under the truck's floodlights just to get the edging and the blowing done before the parking lot filled up, or we had to come back and do it after 5 PM when everyone was going home. 

It just completely scrambled my whole routine. And the days... man, the longer days just completely took over my life. I went from having a normal, predictable route where I’d be pulling the trailer back into the shop by 4:30 in the afternoon, washing down the equipment, and heading home to see my wife, to suddenly being out there twelve, fourteen hours a day, split between early mornings and late evenings. You know, you think you can handle it because it's your business and you've got to keep the client happy, especially a big commercial account like that. You just tell yourself to push through. But it wasn't just the physical hours. It was like the new schedule just swallowed me whole. I’d wake up in the dark, work, sit around waiting to be allowed to work again, and then get home in the dark. 

So, no, I never felt this emptiness before that. Before that, I was tired at the end of the day, but it was a good tired. A satisfied tired. It really all started exactly three years and three months ago when that contract changed and the work just became my entire existence. That's when the heavy feeling moved in, and it just hasn't left since.
